extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students/scholars of Renaissance comic literature
extracted.subtask_description: A full Project Gutenberg edition (translation) of François Rabelais' five-book comic-epic Gargantua and Pantagruel, containing the table of contents and an extended introduction discussing the book's qualities and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of mad mirth and gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: “It stands outside other things--a mixture of mad mirth and gravity, of folly and reason, of childishness and grandeur, of the commonplace and the out-of-the-way, of popular verve and polished humanism, of mother-wit and learning, of baseness and nobility, of personalities and broad generalization, of the comic and the serious, of the impossible and the familiar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book’s value lies in its ability to combine disparate tones and modes (comic and serious, low and high). This blending is presented as a defining strength that produces originality and lasting interest; the introduction treats successful tonal breadth as a positive, distinguishing feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force of life and thought / power of good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: “Throughout the whole there is such a force of life and thought, such a power of good sense, a kind of assurance so authoritative, that he takes rank with the greatest; ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vitality, intellectual vigor, and practical good sense are criteria for praise — the work should display lively imagination combined with thoughtful insight and an authoritative voice that keeps the reader engaged and returns value on re-reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / singularity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: “Had Rabelais never written his strange and marvellous romance, no one would ever have imagined the possibility of its production. It stands outside other things...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is judged positively for its uniqueness and inventive scope; originality of concept and the ability to surprise or transcend conventional forms are highlighted as key merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of learning and popular verve (erudition + wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly emphasizes a combination “of popular verve and polished humanism, of mother-wit and learning,” presenting erudition and scholarly learning integrated with lively popular humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful works in this vein balance scholarly references and classical learning with accessible, witty, popular expression; the combination is considered laudable and part of Rabelais’ achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance (or management) of studied coarseness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great reproach always brought against Rabelais is not the want of reserve of his language merely, but his occasional studied coarseness, which is enough to spoil his whole work, and which lowers its value.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarseness or grossness in language/imagery is identified as a substantive negative: where the author’s language becomes gratuitously filthy it can damage the overall work. The introduction also notes that classical precedents (Aristophanes, Catullus, Petronius, etc.) complicate judgments, so historical/contextual justification may mitigate criticism, but gratuitous filth is an anti-pattern.
